items.title: Creating Durable Background Job Queues for Game Renewal Reminders
items.summary: The short answer For a game renewal notice, the queue is not the system of record. Store the reminder intent and its business deadline in durable state, enqueue a small wake-up job, and make the worker re-check that state before sending. The retry path should preserve the deadline, count attempts, quarantine poison messages, and expose enough history for an operator to recover a missed notice. The useful unit is therefore a recoverable reminder, not a delayed message. A queue can wake a worker; it cannot decide whether a renewal is still eligible after a subscription change, a clock correction, or an outage. In a Node.js service, I would keep the event-loop work small and push delivery to workers, but I would make the same storage and recovery rules apply no matter which queue implementation sits behind the interface. The deadline is a business fact. The delivery timestamp is an attempt. Mixing those two is how a harmless retry becomes a late, duplicate message. The first design mistake is easy to make: treating the delayed message as the reminder itself. The message is only a pointer to work. In a Node.js fintech calling service, list participants before deleting a room, make deletion idempotent, and run a scheduled sweep over rooms that the callback missed. items.summary: Short answer: for a gaming app moving large media, let the browser send bytes to private object storage with a short-lived presigned PUT, and make Node.js or Express sign and confirm the handoff. Keep signed download URLs on the read path. The decision is about access control versus delivery simplicity: the API should authorize the object, while storage carries the file. That boundary is a capacity decision. A proxy makes every slow player connection consume an API worker, socket, and egress path. A direct upload makes the control plane handle short requests while the storage service handles the long transfer. I put separate SLOs on those paths: signing and confirmation latency belong to the API SLO; upload completion and download time belong to the data path. They fail differently. Keep the bucket private. No public shortcut. Treat the upload as a four-step state transition: authorize, reserve, transfer, confirm. The authenticated API decides the object key and allowed content type. It records a pending row, returns a presigned PUT URL and the exact headers to send, and never accepts a client-selected key as authority. React then uploads the file directly. items.title: Microsoft Removes PC-to-PC Migration from Windows 11, Points Users to OneDrive-Based Backup
items.summary: Windows 11 offered a PC-to-PC Migration feature that "moved files and settings directly between two PCs over Wi-Fi or Ethernet," reports Ghacks. But according to an updated Microsoft support page, the tool is no longer available. "Microsoft's support documentation now redirects users to Windows Backup, a tool that relies on OneDrive cloud storage instead of a direct connection between two computers..." Windows Backup works differently. It requires a personal Microsoft account and backs up supported folders (Desktop, Documents, Pictures, Videos and Music) to OneDrive. Free OneDrive accounts include only 5GB of storage, and Microsoft's own promotional screenshot for Windows Backup shows 4.5GB of that allowance already in use. Years of photos, documents and downloads can exceed the free tier quickly. Windows Backup does carry some extras. It can remember installed apps, Wi-Fi networks, passwords and some settings to speed up setup on a new device. Apps still have to be reinstalled, and supported files are restored from the cloud. Thanks to Slashdot reader joshuark for sharing the article. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Rollup to Rolldown without breaking the build contract
items.summary: Swapping a bundler is easy. Knowing what you promised your consumers is the hard part. I migrated two packages of our design system (cortex-core and cortex-react) from Rollup to Rolldown. Before touching the tool, I wrote down the output contract: ESM with preserveModules in dist/esm types generated by tsc in dist/types default.css copied at the end of the build All of it stayed the same. Rolldown's config API is Rollup-compatible and the copy plugin's buildEnd hook still works. The two config files went from 42 and 45 lines down to 18 and 28. Two decisions worth recording: I dropped the CJS output, since both packages were already ESM-only, and I now clean dist before building so a stale artifact never gets published. The cost showed up 13 days later: the mobile Storybook stopped rendering with the new bundle's external packages, and the fix touched the Rolldown configs and added a browser shim to the React Native playground. Lesson: the contract I wrote covered whoever consumes the library, but not whoever consumes the bundle inside our own playground. When you change a build tool, which consumer do you forget to list?

items.title: I Built a Weather-Aware Truck Router with React and Django (and Why the Fastest Route Isn't Always the Right One)
items.summary: If you're driving a car, the fastest route is usually the best route. If you're driving a fully loaded 18-wheeler, 45 mph crosswinds or a band of heavy snow somewhere along the way can turn "fastest" into "dangerous" fast. So I built Weather-Aware Truck Routing: a web app that takes a trip, gets three truck routes, checks the weather at every checkpoint for the hour the truck will actually be there, scores the risk, and recommends the safest route. Drive time is only used as the final tie-breaker. [A] lot of employers are going about it the wrong way, said Arvind Karunakaran, an assistant professor of management science and engineering at Stanford University. "You can consume a lot of tokens without creating a lot of value," Karunakaran said.... The same report, though, found that one-third of organizations surveyed expected AI-related staff reductions in the coming year. items.title: CmdStarter 1.0: Super Easy CLI integration
items.summary: System.CommandLine 2.0 is stable at last, and it is a good parser. What it does not do is decide how your commands are organized in code. You still write the Command objects, the Option objects, the handlers and the wiring between them. CmdStarter is a layer over System.CommandLine 2.0.14 that does that wiring from plain C# code: a class becomes a command, its public properties become options, the parameters of its handler become arguments. Version 1.0.0 is out on NuGet, for .NET 10. I maintain CmdStarter. This article shows what the library does in 1.0, feature by feature, with the code of the samples that ship in the repository, and ends with what changed since the 0.9 betas. System.CommandLine handles parsing, help, completions and the exit codes of parse errors. CmdStarter handles everything around it: it finds the commands in your assemblies, at compile time through a generated catalog or at run time through reflection; it builds the command tree from your namespaces, your attributes or a tree written in code; it creates the System.CommandLine symbols from your properties and parameters, with their default values and their validators; at execution, it creates a fresh instance

items.summary: "I didn't think a rock like this existed on Earth," a geologist at the Lunar and Planetary Institute in Texas told the Washington Post. It looks like a polished rock, dark brown with a clay-colored stripe — but it's actually one of the oldest Mars meteorites ever found, blasted by an impact from the surface of Mars billions of years ago: Technically speaking it's a collection of eight rock fragments, the largest of which is about the size of a fist. Nearly two pounds of the meteorite was discovered in the Sahara in Mali in 2022, and most is now held by a museum in Maine. Within two years, an initial examination determined the meteorite hailed from Mars; scientists are now finally digging deeper, with stunning results. It offers records of "interactions of water and rock and maybe even an imprint of the Martian atmosphere as it was losing water," says Lee Saper, co-author of a new paper recently published in Science. items.title: List`1[System.Int32] is not a style: escaping interpolated values in Spectre.Console markup
items.summary: Spectre.Console uses square brackets for markup: [red]error[/] prints "error" in red. Any literal [ in your text has to be escaped as [[, otherwise the parser tries to read it as a style. MarkupInterpolated and MarkupLineInterpolated exist so you don't have to think about that for values you interpolate. You write $"Hello {name}" and the library escapes name for you. Issue #1763, opened by @yaakov-h, showed that this only worked when the value was a string. My fix is #2118, merged on 12 May 2026 and released in 0.56.0. The issue's repro is short: class CoolThing { public override string ToString() => "This[contains, braces]."; } AnsiConsole.MarkupLineInterpolated($"I have a {thing}"); // InvalidOperationException: Could not find color or style 'contains,'. The detail I liked most in the report was the workaround. Calling {thing.ToString()} yourself avoids the crash, but the IDE then flags it with IDE0071, "simplify interpolation", because an explicit ToString() inside an interpolation hole is normally redundant. So the code the analyzer wants is the code that crashes. All the interpolated APIs go through one method: internal static string EscapeInterpolated(IFormatProvider provider

items.title: Fixing a streaming SwiftUI chat hang: stable scroll anchors and local/cloud cancellation
items.summary: In a SwiftUI reference app, streamed model output and illustrated answer cards repeatedly change the transcript’s height. The assistant uses Apple Foundation Models when available, with a consent-controlled online fallback. A reproduced layout hang led to changes in both rendering and task lifetime. The failure Opening “Ask guide” from an entry could leave the process hung at roughly 99% CPU. The sampled main thread repeatedly hit SwiftUI lazy-stack placement/graph updates, and the observed process footprint reached 1.1 GB. Reopening returned to the same hung process. A UI reproduction also timed out while querying the app. The transcript combined lazy height estimation, a scroll target on a growing answer, animated scrolling, and frequent streamed-text updates. This was a reproduced layout hang; I wouldn't generalize it into “LazyVStack is bad for chat.” What changed A measured VStack replaced the lazy transcript stack. Every exchange gets a separate fixed-height anchor before its changing content. Inserting an exchange triggers one nonanimated scroll to that anchor. items.title: .NET 8 and 9 Are Almost Out of Support. Time to Get Moving.
items.summary: Well, this is awkward. .NET 8 and .NET 9 are both reaching end of support on November 10, 2026. That's right around the corner. If you're still running either version in production, it's time to start thinking about that upgrade. And no, ignoring the calendar doesn't count as an upgrade strategy. I've checked. Microsoft has lined up the end-of-support dates for both releases: Version Release type End of support .NET 8 LTS November 10, 2026 .NET 9 STS November 10, 2026 .NET 10 LTS November 2028 .NET 8 is an LTS release, normally supported for three years. .NET 9 is an STS release, and its support period was extended to 24 months. The result? Both versions get shown the door on the same day. After November 10: No more regular security updates. No more servicing fixes. No more Microsoft technical support for those releases. Your applications won't suddenly stop working at midnight. They'll keep running. But they'll be running on an unsupported platform, and any newly discovered vulnerabilities won't get patched through the normal support lifecycle. That's not a great place to be. items.title: Show HN: Coldframe, a honeypot that poses as a supermarket fridge controller
items.summary: I built Coldframe, a honeypot that pretends to be a supermarket refrigeration controller. Inspired by the events on industrial fridge installations in the past weeks, I wanted to see what people would try against a convincing fake. To learn more about this I built a honeypot that resembled perfectly the Danfoss AK-SM 800A and Dixell XWEB interfaces. Both of them are recognized on Shodan as real ones (an not as honeypots). It’s one Python file using only the standard library, and it builds on eppser/danfoss-ak-sm-decoy and public research by Synacktiv, Claroty and Ironhackers. Things that were fun to get right: - Matching real units. I used Shodan records of real devices to match header order, page titles, certificate fields and TLS versions. The Danfoss persona sends nginx headers in the same order as a real AK-SM 800A. The Dixell persona sends no Server header and pads its page to exactly 8,202 bytes. - Recognising exploit attempts. It recognises CVE-2025-41450, the Danfoss “code of the day” login bypass, and records whether the submitted code is correct for today. AlmaLinux recognized that many community members employed older hardware that relied on x86-64-v2. items.title: A zero is not a measurement until you have run the positive control
items.summary: Everything below reads public files in dotnet/aspnetcore through the GitHub API. No clone, no build, no credentials beyond a logged-in gh. I ran each of these on 7 Nov 2026 against main. gh api "repos/dotnet/aspnetcore/contents/eng/test-configuration.json?ref=main" \ -H 'Accept: application/vnd.github.raw' Swap ?ref=main for ?ref=release/11.0 to check the shipping branch. Both end the same way: "failOnRules": [ ], "quarantineRules": [ ] } quarantineRules is empty. failOnRules is empty. Count the rules and all 14 are in retryOnRules, with localRerunCount: 3 above them. So every rule in this file weakens a guard by allowing reruns; none of them switches a test off. That distinction is the whole point — a retried test still fails the build when it fails deterministically. Note the Accept: application/vnd.github.raw header. Without it the contents API hands you base64 and you have to pipe through base64 -d, whose flag differs across platforms. The raw header avoids that entirely. gh api "search/code?q=QuarantinedTestAttribute+repo:dotnet/aspnetcore" --jq '.items[].path' That returns several paths; the definition is src/Testing/src/xunit/QuarantinedTestAttribute.cs. items.title: Rate limiting in Minimal APIs with .NET's built-in middleware
items.summary: This post was originally published in Portuguese on my blog: Rate limiting em Minimal APIs com o middleware nativo do .NET. Every API exposed to the internet will, sooner or later, get a client that decides to hit the same endpoint a thousand times per second. It might be a bug in a retry loop, a poorly written script or someone trying their luck. If you have no limit at all, the database, the CPU and your other users pay the bill. The good news is that since .NET 7, rate limiting ships with the framework. No extra package, no third-party library. In this post I build a small example with Minimal APIs, per-IP limits, a 429 response with Retry-After and integration tests. The middleware works with two concepts: the limiter (the algorithm: fixed window, sliding window, token bucket or concurrency) and the partition (who is being limited). Without a partition, the limit is global, and one abusive client takes the service down for everyone. Partitioning by IP gives each client its own bucket. You register a named policy and then apply it to the endpoints that need it. Endpoints like health checks usually stay out, otherwise the orchestrator may decide your application is down. builder.

items.title: Put the Mongo-to-SQL toggle at the contract, not inside the shared package
items.summary: We are moving a feature from MongoDB to SQL. One team owns the Mongo side. A different team owns the SQL side. Both want the same common package and the same Function App, with as little code change as possible, and a simple toggle to switch between them. The obvious design is an if (useSql) somewhere. The question is where it lives. I think most people put it in the wrong place. The tempting spot is inside the shared package. One OrderService, one repository class, and a flag that picks the Mongo driver or the SQL client halfway down the call. It feels minimal. One file changes. It is also the version where two teams edit the same class. The Mongo team knows nothing about your SQL joins. The SQL team has never seen your aggregation pipeline. Within a month the flag has leaked into three methods, the tests need both databases running, and nobody can delete the Mongo branch because nobody is sure what it still covers. A toggle inside shared code means the shared code now has two owners and no owner. Put the toggle at the seam. items.title: How are you dealing with all the negative side effects of AI on the web?
items.summary: It seems to me that the AI hype killed the web for good, but not for the reasons we immediately associate with it. Search engines now rank links full of slop at the top, which ironically make LLM summaries acceptable, not because they are better than what we had before (they are not), but because they at least mention the good links which are now buried at the bottom of the page. Also, they've been rate limiting ordinary users like crazy: more often than I'd like to, Google and DuckDuckGo now either show me either an error message or tell me to wait a bit. Sometimes I waste at least a minute refreshing the page and waiting for a result. I also can't browse GitHub freely without being logged in. Anubis is now everywhere, occasionally blocking me. I feel like my productivity has actually gone down thanks to all of that. items.title: I Parsed the Same Format String Five Million Times
items.summary: I had an exporter writing CSV lines, one per row, millions of rows a night. Nothing clever in it: a string.Format call with a template and three values. It was slower than it should've been, so I put a profiler on it, and the call that lit up wasn't the file write or the decimal math. It was the formatting. Specifically, it was the part of string.Format that reads the template "{0},{1:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss},{2:F2}" and figures out where the holes are. That work was happening on every single call, and my template never changed. When you call string.Format(format, args), the runtime has to walk that format string, find the {0}, {1:...}, {2:...} placeholders, pull out the alignment and the format specifiers, and only then start stitching the output together. That parsing step is pure overhead if the template is a constant, which it almost always is. You wrote the template once in your source code. The runtime rediscovers its structure five million times. CompositeFormat is the fix, and it's about as simple as it gets. You parse the template once into a CompositeFormat object, then hand that object to string.Format instead of the raw string. items.title: A New JsonSerializerOptions Every Call Cost Me 120x
items.summary: A list endpoint on one of my services started showing up heavier in the traces than it had any right to be. It pulled a small object, serialized it, returned it. The payload was tiny — an order with three line items. But under load the thing allocated like it was streaming a video, and the CPU time didn't match the shape of the work. I went looking for the expensive query. There wasn't one. The expensive part was the return. Here's the line I'd written, more or less, inside the handler: var json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, new JsonSerializerOptions { PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase, DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull, Converters = { new JsonStringEnumConverter() }, }); Looks fine. It is not fine. That new JsonSerializerOptions { ... } sitting inside a method that runs on every request is the whole bug. I used to think JsonSerializerOptions was a settings bag — a few flags, a naming policy, done. It isn't. items.title: Vibrating Mattress Helps Clear Alzheimer's Protein From the Brain
items.summary: A vibrating mattress combined with two pills that release nitric oxide enhanced the brain's ability to clear an Alzheimer's-related protein. According to New Scientist, the experiment "caused the brain's blood vessels to swell and constrict more strongly, which enhanced the glymphatic system's clearance of [the protein]." From the report: [Kesa Kiviniemi at the University of Oulu in Finland] and his colleagues recruited 29 adults who hadn't been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease or any other cognitive issues. The participants took a pill that dissolves when under the tongue, releasing nitric oxide. They then lay on a mattress that caused their bodies to gently vibrate for 40 minutes, taking another pill halfway through. Blood samples revealed that their levels of a type of protein called beta-amyloid 42 increased by 35 per cent, on average, after the intervention. This protein, which usually helps neurons signal and connect to each other, misfolds and form clumps in Alzheimer's disease. items.title: Freezer meltdowns and airline hoaxes are a taste of things to come. Hoping for the best is no longer an option | Elisabeth Braw
items.summary: Acts of greyzone aggression aim to spread panic. Europe has to show the saboteurs that we are resilient It was as though a ghostly hand had switched the settings on supermarket freezers across Europe from “freeze” to “defrost”. From Finland to Ireland, they suddenly began heating up, many reaching 50C and food worth millions of euros had to be thrown away. But no actual hand was needed to cause the meltdown. This was a cyber-attack, or rather a chain of attacks. Like pretty much everything else in 2026, supermarket freezers are digitally enabled. That makes them smarter and more efficient, but like everything else that is connected to the internet, it also makes them more vulnerable. Russian hacktivists claimed they were behind some of the supermarket sabotage, but no one knows for sure. It could also be Iran, Iranian proxies, North Korea – or unaffiliated bedroom hackers. items.title: Day 14: Extension Points on a Business Object and When to Override Them
items.summary: Behavior a definition can express needs no code written at all. The ones it cannot express are what needs taking over: what to check before this document is submitted, who to notify after it is saved, and under what circumstances a delete is not allowed. The way the framework offers to take over is inheriting from a business object and overriding a few of its steps. A subclass adds this form's own logic at the matching step as required, and the hard part is judging which step is the matching one, and whether that code belongs before or after base. A method name can only answer the order, with DoBeforeSave before the save and DoAfterSave after it. The rest has to be stated by the framework. items.title: How I built a Wordle-style daily puzzle in SwiftUI (no backend)
items.summary: I recently shipped Gemdoku: Daily Block Puzzle, a 9×9 block puzzle for iPhone. The core feature is a Wordle-style Daily Challenge: every player in the world gets the same goal, the same move limit and the exact same sequence of pieces each day. It turned out to be a fun little engineering problem. Here's how it works under the hood, all in plain Swift and SwiftUI, with no backend. The obvious way to give everyone the same puzzle is to generate it on a server. I didn't want a backend. The game is fully offline, has no accounts and collects no data. When the clock strikes midnight, the lavish 4K Switch 2 remake of beloved N64 classic The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will be released, and I have joined a lengthy queue of about 500 fans desperate to snag early copies. There are similar events taking place across the world, from Melbourne to Mexico City; at key locations, Nintendo has senior executives waiting at the tills. items.title: Mining 14,351 Chess Puzzles with Stockfish 18 (and the Illegal-FEN Trap in chess.js)
items.summary: When we started building Brass Pawn (source on GitHub, AGPLv3), we needed a large offline tactics, positional judgement, and endgame dataset that ran completely on-device—both in the browser and natively on iPhone, iPad, and Mac. Transcribing chess puzzles by hand or scraping unverified problem collections breaks down fast. Two failure modes show up immediately in real training: Cooked solutions: A position has a flashy sacrifice, so a human annotator marks it as winning—missing a quiet defensive resource at depth 18, or missing a second equally winning move that punishes a student for playing an objectively strong alternative. Horizon flips: A shallow engine pass (depth 10–12) flags a move as +2.10, only for depth 22 to reveal perpetual check (0.00). Instead of transcribing puzzles, we built a deterministic mining and independent verification pipeline powered by Stockfish 18. Along the way, we hit a subtle FEN validation edge case in chess.js that silently breaks UCI engines. A good tactics puzzle isn't simply "someone blundered in a game." items.title: Making a SwiftUI app survive a folding iPhone: what broke on the iPhone Duo and how I fixed it
items.summary: I make PawLife, a small pet health app (feeding plans in grams, a health diary, a food safety lookup). It is one SwiftUI codebase for iPhone, iPad, Mac Catalyst, Apple Watch and visionOS. When Xcode 27.2 shipped simulators for the iPhone Duo, I expected "it is just a wider iPhone". It is not. Here is what actually broke, in the order I found it, and what the fixes looked like. The Duo has an outer display and an inner one across the fold. Your app runs on one of them at a time, and the window changes size when the user folds or unfolds. The simulator reports it as a window resize, not a new scene. Measured on the simulator: Folded: a 466×678 pt window, of which my app got 382 pt of width. The remaining 84 pt on the trailing edge is a reserved column (status area and camera) exposed through the safe area. Open: a landscape 951×669 pt window, 867 pt for the app, with the same 84 pt trailing column. So the app goes from a narrow portrait phone to a wide landscape slab and back, live, without a relaunch. items.title: iOS silent push not working: content-available and background pushes
items.summary: A silent push, which Apple calls a background notification, has no alert, sound or badge. It wakes your app so it can fetch new content. Apple treats it as low priority and does not guarantee delivery, so "it worked once and then stopped" is often the system working as designed. This page goes through what must be right on the sender and in the app, and what the device itself decides. What you see Likely cause Fix Never arrives, alert pushes work Remote notifications background mode not ticked Signing and Capabilities > Background Modes > Remote notification Shows a banner instead of waking the app quietly alert, sound or badge in aps next to content-available Send aps with content-available: 1 and nothing else APNs returns 400 apns-priority: 10 with apns-push-type: background Priority 5 for background pushes, always Delivered late, or in bursts Priority 5 pushes are sent according to the device's power state Expected; use an alert push for anything a person waits for Arrives in testing, then stops Throttled: too many background pushes Two or three an hour at most Nothing after the user swiped the app away The app was force quit Nothing to fix; it wakes again once the user opens it

items.summary: Nintendo Switch 2; Nintendo This ambitious remake transforms a landmark Zelda game into a modern masterpiece, clearer and easier to navigate, more beautiful to look at, with playful musical touches. Yet the melancholy remains It’s always a worry, returning to a formative piece of art from your childhood. Will your jaded adult sensibilities render you unable to locate the magic that captivated your child self? Will revisiting it reveal that it was never actually that good, and that your tastes are built on a foundation of lies? With video games, there is the added complication of technological advancement: decades-old games can look so basic and feel so treacly to play that it’s hard to explain why they were mind-blowing at the time. Light-touch remasters aim to bring such games up to modern graphical standards without fundamentally changing them; an ambitious remake attempts to transform the work into something that can stand alongside any modern masterpiece. items.title: Interpolative Software (5 minute read)
